vopros: Should I pay for a tool that tracks whether ChatGPT and other AI assistants mention my business, or hire someone to get my business recommended by AI?

vyzhimka.tekst:
Potentially, but I’d separate “measurement” from “optimization.” For most small or midsize businesses, I would not start by paying someone who promises to “get you recommended by ChatGPT.”

AI recommendations aren't a conventional ranking you can reliably buy your way up. ChatGPT Search can discover and cite public sites, and OpenAI specifically recommends allowing OAI-SearchBot, but OpenAI doesn't offer businesses a general mechanism for purchasing organic recommendations. ([help.openai.com](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/12627856?utm_source=openai)) Google similarly says that the fundamentals for its generative AI results are largely the same fundamentals used for Search, and explicitly warns against supposed GEO/AEO hacks and inauthentic mentions. ([developers.google.com](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/ai-optimization-guide?utm_source=openai))

A tracking tool can be useful, but think of it as market research rather than a precise equivalent of Google rank tracking. AI answers can vary with the exact prompt and system being used, so “you rank #4 in ChatGPT” can create a false sense of precision. I'd pay for one when AI-referred customers could be economically meaningful to you and the tool shows the actual prompts it tests, competitors mentioned, citations/sources, results over time, and differences among ChatGPT, Gemini, Copilot, etc.

Before spending much, I'd do a baseline audit. Ask 20–50 realistic questions a prospective customer would ask, such as “best [service] in Los Angeles,” “alternatives to [competitor],” “who can help me with [problem],” and “best [product] for [specific situation].” Record whether you're mentioned, which competitors appear, and—more importantly—which websites the assistants use as sources. That last piece often tells you what you can actually work on.

Then invest in improving the underlying signals assistants can find: a crawlable and technically healthy site; clear pages explaining exactly who you serve and what you're good at; accurate business/product information; legitimate reviews and third-party coverage; authoritative mentions and citations; original expertise, comparisons, FAQs, pricing or other useful information where appropriate; and conventional SEO. OpenAI says allowing its search crawler is necessary for your pages to be included in ChatGPT summaries/snippets, while Google says unique, useful, people-first content and traditional SEO remain foundational for generative search. ([help.openai.com](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/12627856?utm_source=openai))

There are also increasingly useful first-party measurements. For example, Bing Webmaster Tools introduced AI Performance reporting in 2026 for citations across Microsoft AI experiences, while OpenAI says you can measure referral traffic from ChatGPT in your normal analytics. ([blogs.bing.com](https://blogs.bing.com/webmaster/February-2026/Introducing-AI-Performance-in-Bing-Webmaster-Tools-Public-Preview?utm_source=openai)) That means you shouldn't automatically assume you need an expensive dedicated monitoring platform.

If you hire someone, I'd hire a strong SEO/content/digital-PR person who understands AI discovery, rather than someone selling a mysterious proprietary “GEO” technique. Be particularly skeptical of guarantees such as “we'll make ChatGPT recommend you,” paid networks of fake mentions, hundreds of AI-generated pages, or claims that they have special access to AI ranking algorithms. Google specifically notes that third-party tools don't have access to its internal ranking systems and can't guarantee results. ([developers.google.com](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/third-party-seo?utm_source=openai))

If you tell me what kind of business you have, your approximate annual revenue or marketing budget, and whether you're local, ecommerce, SaaS, professional services, etc., I can tell you whether I'd spend $0, a few hundred dollars a month on tracking, or several thousand on actually improving AI/search visibility—and what I'd buy first.
